think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 29-year-old postpartum woman presenting with chronic, multi-year papulonodular skin lesions that flared during pregnancy, accompanied by persistent hoarseness/dysphonia, mucosal involvement (epiglottic edema, nasal crusting, tongue papules), and partial madarosis, mimicking disseminated deep fungal infections, secondary/tertiary syphilis, or severe dermatoses.
2. Admission Breakpoint: Clinical evaluation at the university referral hospital, including dermatologic examination, slit-lamp/ophthalmology exam, and indirect laryngoscopy revealing epiglottic edema and vocal cord involvement, prior to cutaneous wedge biopsy, histochemical staining, and slit skin smear microscopy.
3. Differential Distinctions: Disseminated deep fungal infection (e.g., blastomycosis, histoplasmosis, sporotrichosis) presents with verrucous or nodular skin lesions and mucosal/laryngeal ulceration, but was ruled out by negative PAS staining; syphilis presents with chronic generalized papulonodular eruptions and mucosal patches, but lacks unilateral madarosis and acid-fast dermal bacillary infiltration; multibacillary lepromatous disease uniquely explains the combination of nodular skin infiltration, madarosis, nasal mucosal crusting, laryngeal edema, and dermal acid-fast bacilli on Wade-Fite and Ziehl-Neelsen stains.
case_prompt: A 29-year-old nursing mother presents for evaluation of generalized skin lesions that have been present for several years. The lesions initially began as painful subcutaneous nodules that intermittently discharged mucoid fluid, with a marked worsening during her last pregnancy (delivered six months prior). Over the past two to three months, the lesions increased in size and number to involve her face, and she developed a persistent sore throat accompanied by progressive dysphonia, occasional fevers, and blurring of vision with a gritty sensation in her left eye. Her husband, three children, and 6-month-old infant are all healthy. On physical examination, numerous papules and nodules are distributed across her extremities and face, accompanied by loss of eyebrow density on the right side. Inspection of the oral cavity reveals erythematous papules on the posterior tongue. Ophthalmic examination shows conjunctival injection in the left eye attributed to an inflamed pinguecula. Otolaryngologic examination reveals grey crusted exudates over the nasal mucosa, and laryngoscopy demonstrates marked edema of the epiglottis and false vocal cords. Neurological examination is entirely normal with no palpable peripheral nerve thickening.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Deep systemic and cutaneous fungal infections (such as paracoccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis, or histoplasmosis) were strongly suspected given the chronic noduloulcerative lesions with mucoid discharge, oral mucosal papules, and laryngeal edema; however, special staining of tissue sections failed to identify fungal elements.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: An initial diagnosis of disseminated deep cutanous mycosis to rule out leprosy was made. A wedge skin biopsy taken from her left arm underwent histopathological evaluation. PAS-staining for fungal elements was negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Psoriasis and secondary/tertiary syphilis were initial diagnostic considerations for the generalized chronic cutaneous eruptions; however, the presence of painful subcutaneous nodules discharging mucoid fluid, partial eyebrow loss (madarosis), nasal mucosal crusting, and laryngeal infiltration are incompatible with psoriasis and ruled out by negative serological and histological criteria.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The skin lesions were initially thought to be psoriasis or syphilis. They had started off as painful growths under the skin which would eventually discharge mucoid fluid.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Skin wedge biopsy demonstrated dermal granulomatous inflammation with abundant bacilli identified on Wade-Fite staining, corroborated by Ziehl-Neelsen slit skin smear microscopy demonstrating numerous acid-fast bacilli, confirming multibacillary lepromatous disease.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Basic hematoxyllin and eosin staining revealed multiple granulomas in the dermis. On further staining with wade-fite, multiple bacilli were seen (Figure 2). This was followed by ZN-stained slit skin smear microscopy which showed numerous acid-fast bacilli. Results of other investigations done are shown in the table below (Table 1). A final diagnosis of multibacillary leprosy was made.

editor_comments: Case strictly adheres to admission breakpoint principles. The case prompt preserves clinical presentation, dermatologic findings, madarosis, and laryngoscopy, while withholding biopsy histology and stain results. Ruled-out candidates reflect explicit textual considerations (disseminated deep cutaneous mycosis, syphilis/psoriasis) supported by verbatim quotes.
